questions.q: In an Azure NSG, when two rules both match the same packet, which rule wins?
options: The rule with the lower priority number, regardless of which rule is more specific
The rule that was created most recently
The more specific rule, regardless of its priority number
Both rules apply simultaneously and their effects are combined
questions.explain: NSG rules are evaluated in priority order, lowest number first, and the first match wins — specificity doesn't override priority order.

questions.q: Which six fields define every NSG rule?
options: Priority, source, destination, port, protocol, and access (allow/deny)
Name, region, resource group, tag, cost center, and owner
Priority, bandwidth, latency, region, SKU, and cost
Source, destination, and action only — there is no priority field
questions.explain: Every NSG rule is defined by its priority, source, destination, port, protocol, and allow/deny access decision.

questions.q: What do Azure's default NSG rules do before you add any rules of your own?
options: Allow traffic from inside the VNet and from the Azure load balancer, and deny everything else inbound
Allow all inbound traffic from the public internet by default
Block all traffic, including traffic between resources in the same VNet
Automatically open ports 80 and 443 to the internet
questions.explain: The built-in default rules (priority 65000+) allow VNet-internal traffic and Azure load balancer health probes, then deny everything else inbound.

questions.q: If an NSG is attached to both a subnet and a VM's NIC, how is inbound traffic evaluated?
options: Against the subnet NSG first, then the NIC NSG — traffic must pass both to get through
Only against the NIC NSG; the subnet NSG is ignored once a NIC NSG exists
Against whichever NSG has the higher total number of rules
Azure does not allow an NSG to be attached to both a subnet and a NIC at the same time
questions.explain: When both exist, inbound traffic is checked against the subnet NSG first and then the NIC NSG; it must be allowed by both to reach the resource.

questions.q: An NSG has a priority-100 rule denying TCP port 22 from everywhere, and a priority-200 rule allowing TCP port 22 from one admin IP. Does the admin's SSH traffic get through?
options: No — the priority-100 deny rule is evaluated first and matches, so the packet is dropped before priority 200 is ever checked
Yes — the more specific rule (a single IP) always overrides a broader rule
Yes — allow rules always take precedence over deny rules regardless of priority
It depends on which rule was created first, not on the priority number
questions.explain: Priority 100 is evaluated before priority 200. Since the deny rule matches first, the traffic is dropped and the priority-200 allow rule is never reached.
